newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Honduras ombudsman unhappy with Argentine response.
newsitem.headline: Honduras ombudsman unhappy with Argentine response.

text.p: The Honduran ombudsman said on Wednesday Argentine authorities had ignored his pleas for help in investigating the role of Argentine agents in the disappearance of suspected leftists in his country.
Requests for meetings with Interior Minister Carlos Corach and army chief Gen. Martin Balza and a petition for access to classified files all went unanswered, Leo Valladares said.

"It was a passive nay," the ombudsman told Reuters on the last day of a week-long visit to Argentina. He said the only government official he had access to was a human rights under-secretary, "but she provided me with no information."

Before coming to Buenos Aires Valladares visited Washington, where he was handed 2,600 pages of declassified State Department files that showed more people could have "disappeared" in the hands of Honduran army death squads than the 184 documented cases, he said last week.

He is probing the role of U.S. Central Intelligence Agency and Argentine military trainers in the 1980s, saying they taught torture and killing to Honduran soldiers. Witnesses have told him Argentine agents have taken part in such acts.

Although Argentine authorities were not forthcoming, he said he got crucial fresh testimony from former civilian agents who said Honduran forces were trained in "annihilation" and other "irregular tactics." He declined to elaborate.
"Despite the official silence, there are many people willing to help reveal the truth," he said.
Valladares says witnesses in Honduras have said Argentine soldiers did the "dirty work" for U.S. CIA agents "who did not want to do things prohibited by their country's laws."

Argentine President Carlos Menem last week repeated earlier pledges to help. The New York Times had urged him to keep his word and blasted the White House for not providing CIA and other sensitive documents.

Valladares said he was not disappointed by the Argentine government's response and would keep working on the case. His Argentine counterpart Jorge Maiorano promised to take up the case and help him get hold of the classified files.

Up to 30,000 people disappeared during Argentina's 1976-1983 "dirty war" against leftist rebels. The Argentine regime was also active in helping to train the military in other Latin American countries at the time.
